arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Iowa contends the 1996 plea colloquy adequately informed the defendant of the dangers of proceeding without counsel.
Iowa asserts the waiver of counsel and the guilty plea were therefore knowing and intelligent.
Tovar argues the modern guilty plea colloquy focuses on the consequences of pleading guilty.
Tovar claims this focus parallels the Patterson case and constitutes an intelligent waiver of counsel.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on whether a guilty plea colloquy sufficiently warned the defendant about the disadvantages of proceeding without an attorney. Iowa claims the process met constitutional standards. Tovar argues the waiver lacked the necessary intelligence and knowledge.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the minimum information required during a plea colloquy. It determines whether courts must explicitly detail the risks of self-representation. The outcome shapes how defendants understand their rights before waiving counsel. It impacts the validity of guilty pleas entered without an attorney.
